articles.description:
A backup job should be judged by a measured restore drill, because a successful object upload says nothing about whether the application can recover within its recovery objectives. Start with an isolated restore, a bounded verification query set, and an alert on the age of the latest verified archive; scheduling the dump is the easy part.
Short answer: run logical exports in a separate worker, compress and store each run under a unique key, then promote it to a recovery point only after an isolated restore and application checks succeed.
The important unit of work is the recovery point, not the file. A file can be complete, readable, and still be useless because it came from the wrong database, was overwritten by a later run, or depends on roles, extensions, migrations, and capacity that w…

When an AI tool stages an empty room, the furniture is the easy part to judge. The hard part is whether the room itself is still the same room. If a window shrank or a wall moved by a hand's width, a buyer will notice at the showing, even if the sofa looks great.

articles.author: Vildanden
articles.description:
Claude Code reads files to help you. That is great, until the file is .env, a private key, or a cloud credentials folder. Permission deny rules let you block those reads outright.
In .claude/settings.json (shared with the team) or settings.local.json (personal), add these entries under permissions.deny:
Read(./.env)
Read(./.env.*)
Read(./secrets/**)
Read(~/.aws/**)
Read(~/.ssh/**)
Deny rules win over allow rules, so even if you later allow broad Read access, these paths stay blocked.
Commit the deny list in .claude/settings.json so every teammate gets it.
Add patterns for your own stack: .pem, terraform.tfstate, service-account.json.
Deny Bash(curl:*) too if you do not want the agent sending data out.
Test it: ask Claude Code to read .env and confirm it is refused.
Use deny for things that must never happen, ask for things like git push that need a human, and allow for safe everyday commands like npm test.
I keep copy-ready Claude Code configs (CLAUDE.md templates, slash commands, hooks, permission rules) in Vildanden Agent Config. There is a free sample: https://justly-mia-429.rehost.page/
articles.title: Keep Claude Code away from your .env files with permission deny rules

articles.author: Tess Ainsley
articles.description:
Two things break at once when agents write most of the code. The number of changes goes up, and each change gets smaller, so the total surface a team has to judge grows while any single diff looks less worth a slow read. The reflex is to make review faster. That does not scale, because the work that grows is not reading speed, it is the count of decisions about whether a change is correct.
The number that decides whether a team keeps up is not lines of code. It is how many changes a person has to judge. LinearB's 2026 software engineering benchmarks, drawn from more than 8.1 million pull requests, put agentic pull requests at a median of 89 lines and 293 lines at the 75th percentile, against 157 lines for unassisted work at the same percentile. They also wait: 17.6 hours at the 75th percen…
articles.title: Reviewing the growing volume of AI-generated code

"What did I miss on Telegram today?" sounds like the perfect question for an AI assistant. As of November 2026, neither Claude nor ChatGPT has a built-in Telegram connector, and most Telegram integrations you will find don't answer that question at all. Here is why, and what works.
Telegram has two very different APIs:
The Bot API. You create a bot, get a token, and the bot receives messages sent to it or posted in groups it was added to. Many "Telegram MCP" connectors use this. It is great for notifications and for talking to a bot, but a bot cannot read your private conversations: it is not you.
The user API (MTProto). A client signs in as your account, with your phone number and the login code Telegram sends you, like a new device. It sees what your Telegram app sees: private chats, gro…
